newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-Nazi moved to house arrest in Italy monastery.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi moved to house arrest in Italy monastery.

text.p: Nazi war crimes suspect Erich Priebke was moved under tight security to house arrest at a Roman Catholic monastery just outside the Italian capital on Friday after nearly 16 months in jail, witnesses said.

The German former SS captain, accused of involvement in Italy's worst World War Two atrocity, was driven through the gates of the San Bonaventura monastery in the hilltop wine town of Frascati in a Carabinieri paramilitary police patrol car.

Priebke, 83, had begun his journey from Rome's Forte Boccea military prison in an armoured van with a motorcycle escort but the vehicle was too high to pass under a low railway bridge near the Franciscan monastery, reporters at the scene said.

Priebke had been in jail since his extradition from Argentina to Italy in November 1995 to face trial for alleged complicity in the murder of 335 men and boys, 75 of them Jews, in an SS massacre at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome.
A military court last year found him guilty of the March 1944 killings but not punishable because of extenuating circumstances which triggered a statute of limitation.

The verdict, which led to a siege of the courtroom by angry protesters, was quashed on appeal last October. A retrial is due to start on April 14, when a second suspect, former SS major Karl Hass, also under house arrest, faces the same charges.
A military court on Monday ruled in favour of a defence request for Priebke to be granted house arrest on grounds of worsening mental health.
Workers at the monastery this week installed iron bars over the window of Priebke's room and fitted bulletproof glass.

The newspaper La Repubblica reported on Friday that the simple room, six metres by six metres with a bathroom off it, had a view of Rome. Police and Carabinieri patrols will provide security around the monastery perimeter.
The Frascati monastery said in a statement that it was accommodating Priebke on Christian grounds.

"We have no intention of expressing ourselves on matters of human justice. We have been asked to provide simple hospitality for a detainee. We wish to receive the man in the spirit of sacred hospitality which the Scriptures teach us," it said.
Priebke and Hass both admit that they shot victims at the Ardeatine Caves but say they would have been killed themselves if they had failed to obey orders.
Victims of the relatives and Jewish groups have expressed dismay at the house arrest provisions for Priebke.

"This is not your average Nazi war criminal," Rabbi Abraham Cooper of the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Center said this week. "He deserves to stay in jail every single day for the rest of his life. Period".
A friend of Priebke, Paolo Giachini, said the monastery had been chosen by military authorities from among three the defence team had proposed.
Priebke has testified that he fled to Argentina in 1948 after escaping from a British prisoner of war camp on Italy's Adriatic coast.
He has said his flight to Argentina, where lived openly with his wife and ran a guesthouse in the Andean resort of Bariloche, was aided by a Roman Catholic priest.
Under Italian law, a suspect under house arrest is confined to the premises where he or she resides and can have physical and telephone contact only with lawyers and close family.
